Propargylic Derivatives for the Switchable Synthesis of S‑Alkyl,
S‑Vinyl and S‑Allenyl Phosphorothioates

ABSTRACT: Herein, we report a photoredox/copper dual-catalyzed selective phosphorothiolation of propargylic derivatives from
easily accessible [P(O)SH] compounds. This reaction provides a general, mild and versatile procedure to synthesize a variety of
synthetically useful S-alkyl, S-vinyl and S-allenyl phosphorothioates selectively from the same set of simple starting materials.
P
hosphorothioates containing a phosphorus−sulfur single
bond (P−S) are widely found in many pharmaceutical
and agrochemical molecules (Scheme 1a).
1
Traditional
methods, such as Michaelis−Arbuzov-type reaction, for the
synthesis of phosphorothioates usually required thiols as the
starting materials, which might suffer from high temperature,
toxicity, and moisture sensitivity of reagents, thus resulting in
harsh reaction conditions, complicated operation, and limited
substrates (Scheme 1b, top).
2
By contrast, S-hydrogen
phosphorothioates [P(O)SH]
3−7
and their salts,
8
regardless
of presynthesized or generated in situ, have been developed as
an important synthon in phosphorothiolation processes under
mild reaction conditions. As a result, this readily available,
stable and low-toxicity [P(O)SH] reagent in phosphorothio-
lation reactions with olefins,
5
terminal alkynes
6
or via 1,5-
hydrogen atom transfer (1,5-HAT) process
7
and so on
3,4,8
provide an important alternative for the synthesis of a variety
of high-value phosphorothioates (Scheme 1b, bottom).
However, the transformations involving [P(O)SH] reagents
are still underdeveloped; therefore, achieving structurally
diverse phosphorothioates from [P(O)SH] compounds
remains a desirable yet challenging goal.
Propargylic derivatives, a kind of redox-active substrate,
could be easily activated to generate propargyl species and its
tautomeric allenyl species.
9,10
Benefiting from the extraordi-
nary reaction characteristics of propargyl radicals, major
advancements have been achieved in the transformation of
propargyl derivatives into functionalized propargylic deriva-
tives
9
or allenes
4,10
via metal-catalyzed coupling reactions.
However, these elegant works are mostly limited to the
intrinsic two-electron mechanism involving an oxidative
addition-transmetalation-reductive elimination process, while
examples involving a visible-light-induced through single
electron transfer (SET) process are scarce.
9d,10j
In continu-
ation of our efforts in copper-catalyzed phosphorothiolation
with [P(O)SH] reagents,
3e,6b,7
we speculated that the reactive
propargyl radicals and their tautomeric allenyl radicals could be
generated from propargylic derivatives via an SET process
which might be suitable for the construction of propargylic or
allenylic phosphorothioates. On the other hand, we doubt that
whether the highly reactive allenyl radicals could interact with
oxygen to generate alkenyl radical
11
which might also be able
to couple with [P(O)SH] reagents to produce vinylic
phosphorothioates (Scheme 1c). The predictable challenges
of this approach include (1) the regioselectivity issue on
formation of aforementioned specific radicals and (2) the
match of the specific radicals with the transition metal species

smoothly delivered the target products (3o-3x) in 80%−97%
yields. The yields were almost impervious to positions of the
substituents on the benzene ring, as demonstrated by 3u-3x.
Naphthyl was also tolerated in this protocol (3y). In addition
to the aryl-containing substrates, substrates with an alkyl (3z)
or trimethylsilyl (3aa) substituent were proven successful for
this transformation. The unsaturated bonds, such as alkynyl
(3r) and alkenyl (3z), tethered to alkyne partners were not
influenced in this radical transformation.
The generality of the method to synthesize (Z)-S-vinyl
phosphorothioates in air was further explored. As shown in
Table 2, phenylpropargyl esters with linear (4a-4c), branched
(4d, 4e) or cyclic (4f-4j) alkyl substituents linked to the ester
unit were all compatible with the protocol to produce
structurally diverse S-vinyl phosphorothioates in generally
good yields. Notably, when phenylpropargyl esters with an aryl
substituent linked to the ester unit were used as substrates,
mixed products (4k, 4l) were obtain. We suspected that these
results might be due to the radical intermediates derived from
these substrates possessing little difference in the electronic
properties, resulting in poor regioselectivity via the radical shift
process. Then a variety of alkyne partners tethered to the
propargyl ester were further examined, and the results showed
that electron-donating groups (Me, Ph, OMe) and electron-
withdrawing groups (COOEt, CF
3
) substituted on the para-,

amenable to deliver the desired products (4m-4r) in generally
good yields. Moreover, other P(O)−SH reagents, including

yields. And an alkylpropargyl ester was also investigated, yet no
desired product 4s was produced.
Then we turned our attention to explore the synthesis of S-
allenyl phosphorothioates.
4
Fortunately, the target S-allenyl
phosphorothioates were successfully accessed by using
propargylic oxalates (5) as the starting material (details see
Table S2). Notably, no propargylic isomer was detected under
these reaction conditions, demonstrating the excellent
regioselectivity of this transformation. As shown in Table 3,
a variety of terminal tertiary propargylic oxalates underwent
phosphorothiolation smoothly to produce diverse trisubsti-
tuted S-allenyl phosphorothioate (6a-6k, 6m, 6n) in good to
excellent yields. No significant yield difference among
propargylic oxalates with cyclic (6a-6c) and acyclic (6d-6k)
substituents was observed, demonstrating the good generality
of this protocol. Tetrasubstituted S-allenyl phosphorothioate
(6l) was also successfully accessed through this protocol.
Furthermore, propargylic oxalates derived from more complex
compounds, such as mestranol and ethisterone, served as
competent substrates to produce the corresponding products
(6m, 6n) in good yields.

provide some insights into the mechanism of this trans-

target product 3f was not isolated and TEMPO-trapped
product 7 was detected by HRMS, indicating that a radical
pathway may be involved in this transformation (Scheme 2a).

In summary, we have developed a photoredox/copper dual-
catalyzed phosphorothiolation between easily accessible [P-
(O)SH] compounds and propargylic derivatives under mild
and operationally simple conditions. Photoinduced formation
of a propargyl radical intermediate has been considered as the
key step for these transformations. This method provides an
efficient protocol for the switchable synthesis of highly valuable
S-alkyl, S-vinyl and S-allenyl phosphorothioates from the same
set of simple starting materials.
